title: Kotlin for the Stripe Android screen
description: A practical Kotlin course for solving Stripe-style Android screen problems with clear syntax, reliable parsing, useful collection operations, and small testable functions. You will move from Swift and Dart patterns to idiomatic Kotlin while keeping money in Long cents and every important result easy to verify.

chapters.title: Syntax, values, and control flow
chapters.summary: Translate familiar Swift and Dart ideas into Kotlin. Practise immutable values, nullable strings, data classes, when expressions, ranges, and integer money calculations.

lessons.title: Kotlin values and small data models
lessons.explanation:
Kotlin uses `val` for a read-only reference and `var` for a reassigned one. Money is safest as a `Long` number of cents, such as `1_999L`. A `data class` gives useful value equality and `copy` for free. Kotlin functions can have default arguments, and a `when` expression returns a value.

Nullable values use a `?`. Call a method safely with `?.`, or choose a fallback with `?:`. Prefer these tools to `!!`, which can throw when the value is null.

lessons.explanation:

fun formatCents(cents: Long): String {
    val sign = if (cents < 0) "-" else ""
    val amount = kotlin.math.abs(cents)
    return "$sign\$${amount / 100}.${(amount % 100).toString().padStart(2, '0')}"
}

fun parseCents(text: String): Long? {
    val trimmed = text.trim()
    val negative = trimmed.startsWith("-")
    val unsigned = if (negative) trimmed.drop(1) else trimmed
    val pieces = unsigned.split(".")
    if (pieces.size > 2 || pieces.any { it.isEmpty() }) return null
    val dollars = pieces[0].toLongOrNull() ?: return null
    val fraction = when (pieces.getOrNull(1)?.length ?: 0) {
        0 -> 0
        1 -> pieces[1].toLongOrNull()?.times(10) ?: return null
        2 -> pieces[1].toLongOrNull() ?: return null
        else -> return null
    }
    val result = dollars * 100 + fraction
    return if (negative) -result else result
}

chapters.title: Strings and parsing
chapters.summary: Turn messy text into predictable Kotlin values. Practise trimming CSV fields, safe numeric parsing, defaults, regular expressions, and small validation algorithms.

lessons.title: Split, trim, and destructure
lessons.explanation:
Kotlin's string helpers are compact: `split`, `trim`, `lines`, `drop`, `filter`, `joinToString`, and `padStart` cover many screen-sized parsing tasks. A CSV-like line can be split and mapped before destructuring:

```kotlin
val parts = line.split(",").map { it.trim() }
val (id, merchant, amountText, card) = parts
```

Destructuring expects enough values, so validate input when rows may be malformed. For numbers, prefer `toLongOrNull()` or `toIntOrNull()` when invalid text should become a result instead of an exception.

chapters.title: The collections toolkit
chapters.summary: Use Kotlin collections to group transactions, total money, count categories, find duplicates, and build deterministic reports with explicit ordering.

lessons.title: Grouping and aggregation
lessons.explanation:
Kotlin's collection operations map closely to Swift and Dart. Use `groupBy` to make piles, `groupingBy { }.eachCount()` to count categories, and `sumOf` for totals. The two-argument form of `groupBy` can group one key with a projected value, which is handy for merchant volume:

```kotlin
txs.groupBy({ it.merchant }, { it.cents })
    .mapValues { (_, amounts) -> amounts.sum() }
```

Keep the result type visible when it makes the intent clearer. `List` and `Map` are read-only interfaces; use mutable collections only when the algorithm needs updates.

chapters.title: Testing Kotlin code
chapters.summary: Learn the screen's testing vocabulary: JUnit 4 tests, exact assertions, and a zero-setup harness. Build a test list that covers examples, empty input, boundaries, invalid rows, duplicates, ordering, and large values.

lessons.title: Assertions and JUnit 4
lessons.explanation:
Android Studio commonly runs Kotlin tests through JUnit 4. A test method has `@Test`, and assertions describe the expected result. `assertEquals` checks values, while `assertTrue`, `assertFalse`, and `assertNull` cover predicates and nullable results. Keep each test focused on one behaviour and use names that explain the rule.

For a fee function, test the verified examples and the invalid-input rule. The test itself is executable documentation: it says that 1,000 cents costs 59 cents in fees, 2,550 cents costs 104 cents, and negative amounts are rejected.

lessons.title: Sealed results and safe parsing
lessons.explanation:
A data class names the fields that belong together. A sealed interface names a closed set of outcomes, so a `when` expression can handle every case without a catch-all `else`.

Parsing is a good place to return a result instead of throwing. Trim fields, validate them, and use `?: return` when a conversion fails. The caller can then separate valid values from useful error messages.

lessons.title: Rolling windows and queue state
lessons.explanation:
`ArrayDeque` is a natural first-in, first-out queue. Add new values at the back and remove old values from the front. A running sum makes a moving average constant-time per update instead of rescanning the whole window.

Time-window rules should be written down before coding. In this course, a timestamp is in seconds and the last 60 seconds are inclusive: keep values in `now - 60..now`.

lessons.title: BFS and Dijkstra
lessons.explanation:
Breadth-first search (BFS) explores a graph layer by layer, so it finds a path with the fewest hops when every edge has the same cost. Keep a `previous` map to reconstruct the path after reaching the goal.

Dijkstra's algorithm is the matching tool when edges have non-negative costs. A `PriorityQueue` visits the currently cheapest known route, and a `best` map discards stale queue entries.

chapters.title: Idiomatic, readable Kotlin

lessons.title: Readable transformations
lessons.explanation:
Idiomatic Kotlin is not a contest to use the most scope functions. Use `let` for a non-null value, `apply` to configure an object, and `also` for a side effect while returning the original value. If nested `it` and `this` make a reader stop, give the value a name instead.

A small parse → model → compute → format pipeline is easy to extend. `data class Payment` gives the rows a name, `groupBy` or `groupingBy` handles the computation, and `toSortedMap` makes output order explicit.

lessons.title: Money without floating-point surprises

Store money as `Long` minor units such as cents. When a rate arrives as text, construct `BigDecimal` from that string, multiply once, round once with `HALF_UP`, and convert back to a `Long`.

A cache should make its expiry rule explicit. Store the value together with the time it was written, and compare the injected current time with that timestamp on `get`.

data class Transfer(val from: String, val to: String, val amount: Long)

fun balanceTransfers(balances: Map<String, Long>, threshold: Long): List<Transfer> {
    val deficits = balances.filterValues { it < threshold }.map { it.key to threshold - it.value }.toMutableList()
    val surpluses = balances.filterValues { it > threshold }.map { it.key to it.value - threshold }.toMutableList()
    val transfers = mutableListOf<Transfer>()
    var deficitIndex = 0
    var surplusIndex = 0
    while (deficitIndex < deficits.size && surplusIndex < surpluses.size) {
        val (to, need) = deficits[deficitIndex]
        val (from, available) = surpluses[surplusIndex]
        val amount = minOf(need, available)
        transfers += Transfer(from, to, amount)
        deficits[deficitIndex] = to to (need - amount)
        surpluses[surplusIndex] = from to (available - amount)
        if (need == amount) deficitIndex++
        if (available == amount) surplusIndex++
    }
    return transfers
}

import java.math.BigDecimal
import java.math.RoundingMode

data class CartLine(val sku: String, val unitPriceCents: Long, val quantity: Int)

fun parseCart(text: String): List<CartLine> = text.split(";").filter { it.isNotBlank() }.map { raw ->
    val fields = raw.trim().split(",").map(String::trim)
    require(fields.size == 3)
    CartLine(fields[0], fields[1].toLong(), fields[2].toInt())
}

fun subtotal(lines: List<CartLine>): Long = lines.sumOf { it.unitPriceCents * it.quantity }

private fun percentDiscount(base: Long, percent: String): Long =
    BigDecimal.valueOf(base).multiply(BigDecimal(percent)).setScale(0, RoundingMode.HALF_UP).toLong()

fun save10(lines: List<CartLine>): Long = subtotal(lines) - percentDiscount(subtotal(lines), "0.10")

chapters.title: Rapid review: Kotlin and Terminal
chapters.summary: A fast review deck built from the verified Kotlin and Stripe Terminal rapid-fire questions.

lessons.title: Kotlin basics and null safety
lessons.explanation: These cards cover the small Kotlin rules that prevent large bugs: choosing `val` or `var`, using ranges and loops, and handling nullable values without crashes.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between `val` and `var` in Kotlin?
options: val is read-only after one assignment; var can be reassigned.
val is for numbers; var is for strings.
val is mutable; var is read-only.
exercises.explanation: `val` declares a read-only reference that can only be assigned once (like Swift `let` or Dart `final`), while `var` declares a mutable variable that can be reassigned.

exercises.prompt: How do you write a `Long` literal for zero or 1,999 in Kotlin?
exercises.explanation: Put a capital `L` at the end: `0L` or `1_999L`.

exercises.prompt: What does the Elvis operator `?:` do?
options: It returns the right side unless both sides are null.
It returns the left side when non-null, otherwise evaluates the right side.
exercises.explanation: It returns the left side if it is not `null`, and evaluates the right side (such as a default value, `return`, `continue`, or `error(...)`) if the left side is `null`.

exercises.prompt: Which Kotlin expression matches Swift's `guard let x = maybeX else { return null }`?
exercises.explanation: `val x = maybeX ?: return null`

exercises.prompt: Why should you avoid `!!` in a Stripe interview?
options: It can immediately throw `NullPointerException` when a value is null.
It converts every value to a string.
It only works inside a `when` expression.
exercises.explanation: Because `!!` crashes immediately with a `NullPointerException` if a value is unexpectedly `null`; using `?:`, `?.`, or `getOrDefault` shows defensive, production-grade coding.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between `0..n` and `0 until n`?
exercises.explanation: `0..n` is inclusive and includes `n`, while `0 until n` is half-open and stops at `n - 1` (like `0..<n` in Swift).

exercises.prompt: How do you count backwards from `n - 1` down to `0` in a Kotlin `for` loop?
exercises.explanation: `for (i in n - 1 downTo 0)` — never `n - 1 .. 0`, which is an empty range!

exercises.prompt: How do you loop over both the index and item of a list?
exercises.explanation: `for ((index, item) in list.withIndex())`

exercises.prompt: After dropping a CSV header with `.drop(1)` and looping with `withIndex()`, what is the original 1-based file line number of row `index`?
exercises.explanation: `index + 2` (because `index` starts at `0`, and line `1` was the header).

exercises.prompt: What is the implicit parameter name for a one-parameter lambda when no name is written?
exercises.explanation: `it` (just like `$0` in Swift).

exercises.prompt: When should you replace an implicit `it` with an explicit lambda parameter name?
options: Only when the parameter is an `Int`.
Whenever lambdas are nested or the lambda is more than one or two lines.
exercises.explanation: Whenever you nest one lambda inside another or when the lambda is more than one or two lines long, so the reader never confuses outer `it` with inner `it`.

exercises.prompt: What is the return type of `TODO("not yet implemented")`?
exercises.explanation: Its return type is `Nothing`, which is a subtype of every type in Kotlin, so placing `TODO()` in any function body allows the function to compile regardless of its declared return type.

exercises.prompt: How do you ignore the second element when destructuring a 3-element list or `Triple`?
exercises.explanation: Use an underscore `_` for the unused position: `val (first, _, third) = triple`.

lessons.title: Strings and numbers
lessons.explanation: String indexing, parsing, integer arithmetic, rounding, and exact decimal handling are frequent interview details. Read each option literally: Kotlin's small type distinctions matter.

exercises.prompt: How do you split a multiline CSV into non-empty data rows after skipping its header?
exercises.explanation: `csv.lines().drop(1).filter { it.isNotBlank() }`

exercises.prompt: How do you split a CSV row by commas and strip spaces around every column?
exercises.explanation: `row.split(",").map { it.trim() }`

exercises.prompt: Why check `cols.size` before `val (a, b, c) = cols`?
options: A list with fewer than three elements causes `IndexOutOfBoundsException`.
exercises.explanation: Because destructuring a list with fewer than 3 elements throws an `IndexOutOfBoundsException` immediately.

exercises.prompt: What does `"fr-CA".substringAfter("q=", missingDelimiterValue = "1")` return?
exercises.explanation: It returns `"1"`, because `"q="` is not present in `"fr-CA"`, so `missingDelimiterValue` supplies the fallback instead of returning `"fr-CA"`.

exercises.prompt: How do you convert `"2550"` to a `Long` without risking `NumberFormatException`?
exercises.explanation: `"2550".toLongOrNull()`, which returns `2550L` on valid digits and `null` on `"abc"`.

exercises.prompt: How do you format 5 cents as the two-character string `"05"`?
exercises.explanation: `5.toString().padStart(2, '0')`

exercises.prompt: What lesson explains why a `formatCents(0)` implementation returned an empty string?
options: Padding only works for positive `Int` values.
An unnecessary `if (cents != 0L)` skipped the formatting logic; zero should be tested.
exercises.explanation: Because of an unnecessary `if (cents != 0L)` guard around the formatting logic; the lesson is to let general math handle `0` (`0 / 100` is `0` and `0 % 100` padded is `"00"`) and always write a test for `0`.

exercises.prompt: When splitting dollar strings such as `"12.05"` and `"12"`, why check `parts.size > 2` rather than `parts.size != 2`?
options: A whole-dollar string has one valid part and no decimal point.
A decimal string always produces three parts.
`split` always returns an empty list for `"12"`.
The comparison is only needed for negative amounts.
exercises.explanation: Because a whole-dollar string like `"12"` has no decimal point, so `split(".")` produces `parts.size == 1`, which is valid when whole dollars are allowed!

exercises.prompt: Which expression computes basis points out of 10,000 using rounded half-up `Long` math?
exercises.explanation: `(amountCents * basisPoints + 5_000) / 10_000`

exercises.prompt: How do you get the length of a `String` versus the size of a `List` or `Map`?
options: Use `.size` for strings and `.length` for collections.
Use `.length` for strings and `.size` for lists, sets, and maps.
Use `.count` for strings and `.length` for maps.
exercises.explanation: On a `String`, use `.length` (a property, no parentheses). On a `List`, `Set`, or `Map`, use `.size` (also a property, no parentheses).

exercises.prompt: What does `"hello"[1]` return, and what is its type?
exercises.explanation: It returns the character `'e'`, and its type is `Char`.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between `s.substring(1, 4)` and `s.substring(1..4)`?
options: The first end is exclusive; the range end is inclusive.
Both return the same three characters.
The first uses a regex; the second uses bytes.
The first is inclusive; the range end is exclusive.
exercises.explanation: `s.substring(1, 4)` has an exclusive end index (`4`), returning 3 characters at indices `1, 2, 3`. `s.substring(1..4)` uses an inclusive range `1..4`, returning 4 characters at indices `1, 2, 3, 4`.

exercises.prompt: Does `s.split(".")` use a regular expression or a literal dot?
options: A literal dot; a regex requires explicitly passing `Regex(".")`.
exercises.explanation: A literal dot! In Kotlin, `split` taking a `String` or `Char` always splits on the exact literal delimiter unless you explicitly pass a `Regex(".")`.

exercises.prompt: What does `"".split(",")` return?
options: A one-element list containing the empty string: `[""]`.
exercises.explanation: A one-element list `[""]` containing the empty string, not an empty list!

exercises.prompt: How do you split `"key:val:with:colons"` into at most two pieces around the first colon?
exercises.explanation: Call `"key:val:with:colons".split(":", limit = 2)`, which returns `["key", "val:with:colons"]`.

exercises.prompt: What does `"abc".substringAfter(":")` return when the delimiter is absent?
options: The string before the missing delimiter.
exercises.explanation: By default it returns the original string `"abc"`! Pass a second argument `"abc".substringAfter(":", "")` if you want an empty string when the delimiter is missing.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between `isEmpty()` and `isBlank()`?
options: `isEmpty()` only matches length zero; `isBlank()` also matches whitespace-only text.
`isBlank()` only matches length zero; `isEmpty()` matches whitespace.
exercises.explanation: `isEmpty()` is `true` only when `s.length == 0`. `isBlank()` is `true` when `s` is empty or consists solely of whitespace characters like spaces, tabs, and newlines.

exercises.prompt: How do you pad `"7"` with leading zeros to width 4?
exercises.explanation: `"7".padStart(4, '0')`, which returns `"0007"` (note that `'0'` is a `Char` in single quotes).

exercises.prompt: How do you convert the digit character `'9'` to integer `9`?
exercises.explanation: Call `'9'.digitToInt()`, which returns `9`. Using `'9'.code` returns its ASCII code point `57`.

exercises.prompt: What does `"42a".toIntOrNull()` return?
exercises.explanation: It returns `null` instead of throwing `NumberFormatException`.

exercises.prompt: How can two regex capture groups be extracted directly into two variables?
options: Call `match.groups()` and assign the whole object to two variables.
Regex groups can only be accessed by numeric indices.
exercises.explanation: Match with `Regex("""(\w+)=(\d+)""").matchEntire(input)` (or `.find(input)`) and destructure `.destructured`: `val (key, num) = match.destructured`.

exercises.prompt: What do `-7 / 2` and `-7 % 2` evaluate to in Kotlin?
exercises.explanation: `-7 / 2` truncates toward zero to `-3`, and `-7 % 2` evaluates to `-1`.

exercises.prompt: What does `Math.floorMod(-7, 2)` return?
exercises.explanation: It returns `1`, because floor modulo always takes the sign of the positive divisor `2`.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between `2.5.roundToInt()` and `kotlin.math.round(2.5).toInt()`?
options: The first returns `3`; the second uses half-even and returns `2`.
The first returns `2`; the second returns `3`.
exercises.explanation: `2.5.roundToInt()` delegates to `Math.round` (ties toward positive infinity) and returns `3`, whereas `kotlin.math.round(2.5)` uses half-to-even (banker's rounding) and returns `2.0` (`2` as `Int`).

exercises.prompt: How do you clamp an `Int` fee `f` to the inclusive range 50 through 5000?
exercises.explanation: Call `f.coerceIn(50, 5000)` (or `f.coerceIn(50..5000)`).

exercises.prompt: Why is `BigDecimal("2.0") == BigDecimal("2.00")` false, and how should numeric value be compared?
options: The strings have different signs; use `toDouble()`.
`equals` requires matching value and scale; use `compareTo(...) == 0`.
The values are not equal numerically.
exercises.explanation: `==` calls `BigDecimal.equals`, which requires both value and scale to match (`1` vs `2`). Use `bd1.compareTo(bd2) == 0` to compare numeric value ignoring scale.

exercises.prompt: Why should you construct `BigDecimal` from `"0.1"` instead of `0.1`?
options: A `Double` is always stored as a string.
`BigDecimal` only accepts strings for negative values.
The `Double` already contains binary floating-point error; a string preserves decimal digits.
exercises.explanation: Because `0.1` as a binary `Double` is already slightly inaccurate (`0.10000000000000000555...`). Always pass a `String`: `BigDecimal("0.1")`.

lessons.title: Collections
lessons.explanation: Kotlin collections reward precise choices: know when a collection is mutable, which side of a pair becomes a map key, and whether an operation keeps or drops duplicates.

exercises.prompt: What is Kotlin's equivalent of Swift's `compactMap`?
exercises.explanation: `mapNotNull { ... }`

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between `groupBy { it.id }` and `associateBy { it.id }`?
options: `groupBy` keeps a list for every key; `associateBy` keeps one value and overwrites earlier duplicates.
Both reject duplicate keys with an exception.
exercises.explanation: `groupBy` returns `Map<K, List<T>>` keeping every item with the same key, whereas `associateBy` returns `Map<K, T>` and silently overwrites earlier items if duplicate keys exist!

exercises.prompt: How do you count how many items belong to each category in one expression?
exercises.explanation: `list.groupingBy { it.category }.eachCount()`

exercises.prompt: How do you sort merchants by `netCents` highest-first, then `name` A-to-Z?
exercises.explanation: `merchants.sortedWith(compareByDescending<MerchantSummary> { it.netCents }.thenBy { it.name })`

exercises.prompt: Is Kotlin's `sortedBy` stable?
options: Yes; equal sort keys keep their original input order.
exercises.explanation: Yes, it is stable, meaning items with equal sort keys automatically stay in their original input order.

exercises.prompt: How do you append `tx` to a map bucket whether or not its key already exists?
exercises.explanation: `buckets.getOrPut(tx.card) { mutableListOf() }.add(tx)`

exercises.prompt: In `headers.zip(values).toMap()`, which list becomes map keys?
options: The left list, `headers`; `values` become map values.
exercises.explanation: The left list (`headers`) becomes the keys, and the right list (`values`) becomes the values.

exercises.prompt: How can a `MutableSet<String>` detect a duplicate in one `if` check?
exercises.explanation: `if (!seen.add(id))` — because `MutableSet.add` returns `false` if the element was already in the set!

exercises.prompt: Which collection and methods suit a FIFO queue or timestamp window?
exercises.explanation: Use `ArrayDeque<T>()`, using `addLast(x)` to push to the back and `removeFirst()` to pop from the front (and `first()` to peek at the oldest item).

exercises.prompt: When should you use BFS instead of Dijkstra on a graph?
options: BFS only for negative edges; Dijkstra for equal weights.
BFS for equal-weight steps; Dijkstra for different positive costs.
Always use Dijkstra because BFS cannot use `ArrayDeque`.
Use BFS for sorting and Dijkstra for parsing.
exercises.explanation: Use BFS when every step has equal weight (finding fewest hops), and use Dijkstra when edges have different positive costs (finding cheapest total cost).

exercises.prompt: Does `setOf("b", "a", "c")` preserve insertion order on the JVM?
options: Yes, the default set and map implementations preserve insertion order.
Only sets of integers preserve order.
exercises.explanation: Yes, `setOf` and `mutableSetOf` (as well as `mapOf` and `mutableMapOf`) preserve insertion order by default using `LinkedHashSet` and `LinkedHashMap`.

exercises.prompt: How do you create a list of five zeros without a loop?
exercises.explanation: `List(5) { 0 }`, which calls the lambda for indices `0..4` and returns `[0, 0, 0, 0, 0]`.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between `list.remove(2)` and `list.removeAt(2)` on a `MutableList<Int>`?
options: `remove(2)` removes the last item; `removeAt(2)` removes the first.
exercises.explanation: `list.remove(2)` removes the first occurrence of the integer **value** `2`, whereas `list.removeAt(2)` removes the element at **index** `2`.

exercises.prompt: How do you remove all negative numbers from a `MutableList<Int>` in place?
exercises.explanation: Call `list.removeAll { it < 0 }`.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between `map[key]` and `map.getValue(key)`?
options: Both return a nullable value without throwing.
exercises.explanation: `map[key]` returns `null` if `key` is absent, whereas `map.getValue(key)` throws `NoSuchElementException` if `key` is absent.

exercises.prompt: How do you append `x` to a mutable-list value in a map, creating the list for a new key?
exercises.explanation: `map.getOrPut(key) { mutableListOf() }.add(x)`.

exercises.prompt: How do you increment a possibly missing `Long` balance in a mutable map?
exercises.explanation: `map[key] = map.getOrDefault(key, 0L) + delta`.

exercises.prompt: How do you iterate over both keys and values of a map?
exercises.explanation: Use destructuring in parentheses: `for ((key, value) in map) { ... }`.

exercises.prompt: Which class supports both a FIFO queue and a LIFO stack in pure Kotlin?
exercises.explanation: `ArrayDeque<T>()`, using `addLast(x)` and `removeFirst()` for a queue, or `addLast(x)` and `removeLast()` for a stack.

exercises.prompt: How do you create a max-heap of `Int` with `PriorityQueue`?
exercises.explanation: `PriorityQueue<Int>(compareByDescending { it })` (or `PriorityQueue<Int>(reverseOrder())`).

exercises.prompt: On `TreeMap<Int, String>`, what do `floorKey(50)` and `ceilingKey(50)` mean?
options: Both return the exact key 50 or throw.
They return values rather than keys.
exercises.explanation: `floorKey(50)` returns the greatest key `<= 50` (or `null`), while `ceilingKey(50)` returns the smallest key `>= 50` (or `null`).

exercises.prompt: How do you transform strings into valid integers while dropping parse failures?
exercises.explanation: `strings.mapNotNull { it.toIntOrNull() }`.

exercises.prompt: In `val (a, b) = list.partition { it > 0 }`, which variable gets true matches?
options: `b` gets true matches; `a` gets false elements.
`a` gets true matches; `b` gets false elements.
exercises.explanation: The first variable, `a`, always gets the `true` matches, and `b` gets the `false` elements.

exercises.prompt: What happens when duplicate keys exist in `distinctBy` versus `associateBy`?
options: `distinctBy` keeps the last; `associateBy` keeps the first.
`distinctBy` keeps the first element; `associateBy` keeps the last.
exercises.explanation: `distinctBy` returns a `List` keeping the **first** element for each key, whereas `associateBy` returns a `Map` keeping the **last** element for each key!

exercises.prompt: What are `chunked(3)` and `windowed(3)` on `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`?
options: Both return the same three windows.
exercises.explanation: `chunked(3)` returns non-overlapping batches including the partial tail: `[[1, 2, 3], [4, 5]]`. `windowed(3)` slides by 1 and drops partial windows by default: `[[1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 4], [3, 4, 5]]`.

exercises.prompt: How do you compute adjacent differences for `[10, 13, 20]`?
exercises.explanation: `listOf(10, 13, 20).zipWithNext { a, b -> b - a }`, which returns `[3, 7]`.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between `associateBy` and `associateWith`?
options: Both make elements keys and ignore the lambda.
`associateBy` makes a list; `associateWith` makes a set.
In `associateBy`, elements become values and the lambda computes keys; in `associateWith`, elements become keys and the lambda computes values.
exercises.explanation: In `list.associateBy { keySelector }`, each list element becomes a map **value** and the lambda computes its **key**. In `list.associateWith { valueSelector }`, each list element becomes a map **key** and the lambda computes its **value**.

exercises.prompt: How do you count the frequency of each string in a list?
exercises.explanation: `list.groupingBy { it }.eachCount()`.

exercises.prompt: Why does `emptyList<Int>().reduce { a, b -> a + b }` crash?
options: `reduce` has no initial value; use `fold(0)`, `reduceOrNull`, or `sum()`.
All collection operations reject empty lists.
exercises.explanation: `reduce` has no initial value and throws `UnsupportedOperationException` on an empty collection. Use `fold(0) { a, b -> a + b }`, `reduceOrNull`, or `.sum()`.

exercises.prompt: How do you make `sumOf { ... }` return a `Long` rather than an `Int`?
options: Ensure the lambda expression has type `Long`, such as `it.cents.toLong()`.
exercises.explanation: Ensure the expression inside the `sumOf` lambda has type `Long` (for example, `list.sumOf { it.cents.toLong() }`).

exercises.prompt: What does `emptyList<Int>().all { it > 0 }` return?
options: It throws because the list is empty.
exercises.explanation: It returns `true` (vacuous truth—there are no counterexamples in an empty list!).

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between `maxByOrNull { it.age }` and `maxOfOrNull { it.age }`?
options: The first returns the age; the second returns the element.
Both throw on an empty list.
The first returns the element object; the second returns the maximum age value.
exercises.explanation: `maxByOrNull` returns the **element object** (e.g., `Person?`) that had the maximum age, while `maxOfOrNull` returns the **age value itself** (`Int?`).

exercises.prompt: Does `list.sorted()` modify `list` in place?
options: No; it returns a new sorted `List` and leaves the original untouched.
Yes, all sorting extensions mutate the receiver.
It sorts only if the list is mutable.
exercises.explanation: No! `sorted()`, `sortedBy()`, `sortedDescending()`, and `sortedWith()` all leave the original collection untouched and return a **new** sorted `List`.

exercises.prompt: How do you sort `Item` objects by score descending and then name ascending?
exercises.explanation: `items.sortedWith(compareByDescending<Item> { it.score }.thenBy { it.name })`.

exercises.prompt: Why is `Comparator { a, b -> a - b }` dangerous?
options: Subtracting can overflow `Int`; use `a.compareTo(b)` or `compareBy { it }`.
exercises.explanation: `a - b` can overflow 32-bit `Int` when `a` and `b` have opposite signs and large magnitudes. Always write `Comparator { a, b -> a.compareTo(b) }` (or `compareBy { it }`).

lessons.title: Classes and types
lessons.explanation: Data classes, enums, sealed interfaces, computed properties, and scope functions make domain models both safer and easier to explain in an interview.

exercises.prompt: What four things does putting `data` before `class` provide?
options: Automatic serialization, networking, threading, and caching.
A private constructor, singleton object, and inheritance.
Value equality and hashCode, readable toString, copy(), and destructuring.
exercises.explanation: Value equality (`equals` / `==` and `hashCode`), a readable `toString()`, `.copy()`, and destructuring (`val (a, b) = obj`).

exercises.prompt: What happens when an `expect()` test compares two equal-looking regular class instances?
options: `expected == actual` compares memory addresses, so identical fields can still fail.
The test cannot compile because regular classes cannot be tested.
The objects are always considered equal.
exercises.explanation: `expected == actual` compares memory addresses instead of field values, so the test prints `FAIL` even when both objects hold identical data!

exercises.prompt: How can an enum be parsed safely despite unknown or lowercase input?
exercises.explanation: Write a helper on the enum's `companion object`: `entries.firstOrNull { it.name.equals(text, ignoreCase = true) }`.

exercises.prompt: When should you use an `enum class` versus a `sealed interface`?
options: Enums are for different fields; sealed interfaces are only for constants.
Use enums for nullable values and sealed interfaces for strings.
Enum cases share one shape; sealed subtypes can carry different fields.
They are interchangeable in every model.
exercises.explanation: Use an `enum class` when all cases have the exact same shape (like `CHARGE, REFUND, PAYOUT`), and use a `sealed interface` when different cases carry different fields (like `Ok(val reader: Reader)` vs `Invalid(val line: Int, val reason: String)`).

exercises.prompt: What makes a `when` expression over a sealed interface exhaustive?
options: A sealed interface always has exactly two subtypes.
The compiler inserts a default case that hides missing branches.
All subtypes are known at compile time, so every subtype can be checked without `else`.
exercises.explanation: Because all subtypes are known at compile time, you do not need an `else` branch, and the compiler will flag an error if you ever add a new subtype and forget to handle it in `when`.

exercises.prompt: Why does `val openCount: Int get() = active.size` need `get() =`?
options: It recomputes `active.size` every time the property is read.
It runs only once when the object is constructed.
exercises.explanation: Without `get() =`, `active.size` is evaluated only once when the object is constructed (`0`); with `get() =`, it recomputes `active.size` every time `openCount` is read.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between `require(cond)`, `check(cond)`, and `error(msg)`?
options: `require` means invalid input, `check` means invalid state, and `error` unconditionally throws `IllegalStateException`.
`require` checks state, `check` checks input, and `error` returns a message.
exercises.explanation: `require` throws `IllegalArgumentException` when an input parameter is invalid, `check` throws `IllegalStateException` when an object is in the wrong state, and `error(msg)` unconditionally throws `IllegalStateException` right away.

exercises.prompt: Why do two `class Key(val id: String)` instances with `"k1"` not match as `HashMap` keys?
options: Hash maps compare only object size.
A plain class uses identity equality; use `data class Key(val id: String)` for value equality.
exercises.explanation: A plain `class` uses object memory identity for `equals` and `hashCode`. Prefix it with `data` (`data class Key(val id: String)`) so the compiler generates value-based `equals` and `hashCode`.

exercises.prompt: Which two scope functions return the original receiver object rather than the lambda result?
exercises.explanation: `apply` (which uses `this`) and `also` (which uses `it`)—the two starting with the letter **a**.

exercises.prompt: What does `"  ".trim().takeIf { it.isNotEmpty() }` return?
options: It throws because `takeIf` needs a non-empty value.
exercises.explanation: It returns `null`, because `"".isNotEmpty()` is `false`.

exercises.prompt: Why does `"$user.name"` fail to interpolate the `name` property?
options: Kotlin never supports properties in templates.
Kotlin binds only `$user` and treats `.name` as literal text; use `${user.name}`.
The dot means a nullable call.
exercises.explanation: Without braces, Kotlin only binds the identifier `$user` and treats `.name` as literal text. Wrap the dotted expression in curly braces: `"${user.name}"`.

exercises.prompt: Why does `intArrayOf(1, 2) == intArrayOf(1, 2)` evaluate to false?
options: `==` always means reference identity for lists too.
`==` on arrays checks reference identity; use `contentEquals` or compare lists.
exercises.explanation: `==` on arrays checks reference identity, not element equality. Call `arr1.contentEquals(arr2)` (or use `listOf(1, 2) == listOf(1, 2)`).

lessons.title: Testing and fakes
lessons.explanation: Small seams make interview code testable. Inject time and network behavior, preserve earlier problem parts, and assert failures deliberately.

exercises.prompt: How should you test a 1,000 ms batch flush without `Thread.sleep`?
options: Sleep for 1,000 ms in every test.
Read the system clock directly from the class.
Use a random timestamp until the test passes.
Inject a `Clock` interface and advance a fake clock manually in the test.
exercises.explanation: Define `fun interface Clock { fun nowMillis(): Long }`, inject it into your class's constructor, and pass a `FakeClock(var now: Long = 0)` whose `now` field you advance manually in tests.

exercises.prompt: How can you test retry logic without a real server?
options: Inject a `fun interface` sender and use a fake with scripted results and recorded requests.
Use a production server and retry until it responds.
Catch every exception and skip the test.
Hard-code the final success result in the class.
exercises.explanation: Define a `fun interface` for the sender/uploader and pass a fake backed by an `ArrayDeque` of scripted `SendResult` values (`RETRYABLE`, `SUCCESS`, `PERMANENT`) that also records received requests in a `MutableList`.

exercises.prompt: In `expect(name, expected, actual)`, what are the three arguments in order?
options: Actual result, label, expected right answer.
Label, expected right answer, actual function result.
Label, actual result, expected right answer.
exercises.explanation: First is the string label `name`, second is the `expected` right answer, and third is the `actual` result returned by calling your function.

exercises.prompt: Why should Part 1's test input remain unchanged when Part 2 adds rows or rules?
options: Part 1 tests are never run again.
Changing shared input can break earlier checks; keep `inputPart1` and define `inputPart2` separately.
Later parts may only use empty input.
exercises.explanation: Because changing Part 1's shared input can break Part 1's existing `expect()` checks; always keep `inputPart1` intact and define `inputPart2` separately so all parts stay green.

exercises.prompt: How do you check that an expression throws inside `main()` using `expect()`?
options: `expect("throws on bad input", true, runCatching { myFunction(badInput) }.isFailure)`
exercises.explanation: `expect("throws on bad input", true, runCatching { myFunction(badInput) }.isFailure)`

exercises.prompt: Which characters are forbidden inside backtick `@Test` function names on the JVM?
options: Period `.`, colon `:`, slash `/`, and angle brackets `<` and `>`.
exercises.explanation: Period `.`, colon `:`, slash `/`, and angle brackets `<` `>`.

lessons.title: Problem-solving method
lessons.explanation: These cards turn common interview mistakes into a repeatable method: choose the right graph tool, keep decimal arithmetic exact, and ask what changed between parts.

exercises.prompt: When should a graph solution use BFS versus Dijkstra?
options: BFS handles weighted edges; Dijkstra handles only strings.
BFS handles equal-weight hops; Dijkstra handles different positive edge costs.
Dijkstra is required whenever a graph has cycles.
Use either algorithm; their results are always identical.
exercises.explanation: Use BFS when every step has equal weight (finding fewest hops), and use Dijkstra when edges have different positive costs (finding cheapest total cost).

exercises.prompt: Why must `BigDecimal` receive `BigDecimal("1.37")` rather than `BigDecimal(1.37)`?
options: The constructor accepts only values with two decimal places.
A `Double` cannot be used in Kotlin at all.
The `Double` already contains binary floating-point error; the string preserves exact base-10 digits.
exercises.explanation: Because a `Double` literal already contains binary floating-point error before `BigDecimal` even sees it, whereas a `String` preserves the exact base-10 decimal digits.

exercises.prompt: Why must a payout check the balance before subtracting it?
options: The check is only needed after sorting.
Subtraction automatically rolls back on failure.
Subtracting first can let a rejected payout mutate the balance; validate before mutation.
exercises.explanation: Because it subtracted the payout from the balance *before* checking if the balance went negative; always check `if (balance < amount)` *before* mutating the balance, like an ATM!

exercises.prompt: What four questions should you ask when Part 2 or Part 3 is revealed?
options: Did input change? Did output change? Which rule changed? What new thing must I remember while looping?
Can I delete Part 1? Can I rename every type? Can I skip tests? Can I use `!!`?
Is the code shorter? Is it clever? Is it generic? Is it recursive?
Which IDE theme is active? Which tab is open? Which font is selected? Which key is pressed?
exercises.explanation: (1) Did the input change? (2) Did the output change? (3) Which rule changed? (4) What new thing must I remember while looping?

exercises.prompt: In the Luhn checksum, which digits are doubled and how is a doubled value above 9 handled?
options: Double every digit from the left; add 9 when above 9.
Double every second digit from the right; subtract 9 if the doubled value exceeds 9.
Double only the first digit; divide values above 9 by 2.
Never double digits; sum the card number as a string.
exercises.explanation: Starting from the rightmost digit, you double every second digit (indices 1, 3, 5... from the right), and if the doubled value is greater than 9, you subtract 9; the card number is valid if the sum of all digits is divisible by 10.

exercises.prompt: What payment-card data must never be written to logs or telemetry?
options: Only the last four digits, even when masked.
Full PAN, CVV/CVC, PIN, and raw magnetic-stripe or chip track data.
The payment status and a masked last-four display.
exercises.explanation: Never log the full card number (PAN—only mask to last 4 like `•••• 4242`), CVV/CVC security code, PIN, or raw magnetic-stripe/chip track data.

lessons.title: Payments and Terminal
lessons.explanation: Terminal work combines state machines, retries, and money safety. The safest answer usually preserves one payment identity and makes retries idempotent.

exercises.prompt: Why should money use `Long` rather than `Int` or `Double` in Kotlin?
options: `Double` always stores decimal cents exactly, while `Long` rounds.
`Long` is required only for display formatting.
`Long` stores exact whole cents without floating-point rounding or 32-bit overflow.
exercises.explanation: `Double` has binary floating-point rounding bugs (turning `"19.99"` into `1998` cents), and 32-bit `Int` overflows at around 21 million dollars in cents, whereas 64-bit `Long` holds exact whole cents without overflow or rounding error.

exercises.prompt: What should you do after a Terminal payment is declined, has a connectivity blip, or times out?
options: Reuse the same `PaymentIntent` or check its status on timeout.
Create two new intents and keep the first success.
exercises.explanation: In all three cases, **reuse the same `PaymentIntent`** (or check its status on timeout)—never create a new `PaymentIntent`, because creating a new one after a timeout can authorize the customer's card twice.

exercises.prompt: In Stripe Terminal manual capture (`requires_capture`), how long do you have to capture?
exercises.explanation: Within 2 days.

exercises.prompt: What is an idempotency key, and why is a payment ID useful for offline retries?
options: It encrypts the card number and guarantees every retry charges again.
It is a UI label that has no server meaning.
It lets the server deduplicate retries, so resending payment `p1` returns the original result without charging twice.
It deletes duplicate payments locally but cannot affect the server.
exercises.explanation: An idempotency key is a unique key sent with a request so the server deduplicates retries; if the app crashes after sending payment `"p1"` and resends `"p1"` on restart, the server recognizes key `"p1"` and returns the original result without charging twice.

lessons.title: Interview behaviour
lessons.explanation: The coding screen measures communication as well as code. These cards summarize the allowed tools, the opening routine, and habits for recovering clearly when stuck.

exercises.prompt: Which list contains Stripe's six operating principles?
options: Move fast; win every argument; ship alone; avoid documentation; optimize only for speed; never ask questions.
Users first; maximize revenue; use any tool; skip tests; minimize code; avoid feedback.
Craft; hierarchy; secrecy; perfection; independence; competition.
Users first; Create with craft and beauty; Move with urgency and focus; Collaborate egolessly; Stay curious; Obsess over talent.
exercises.explanation: Users first; Create with craft and beauty; Move with urgency and focus; Collaborate egolessly; Stay curious; Obsess over talent.

exercises.prompt: What are the rules on AI tools, documentation, and search in the Team Screen?
options: AI tools are prohibited, while official documentation, Google, StackOverflow, and the standard library are allowed.
AI answers are required, and documentation is prohibited.
Every search result is allowed, including AI-generated answers.
No tools or references of any kind are allowed.
exercises.explanation: AI tools are strictly prohibited (including Gemini in Android Studio and AI answers in search results), while official documentation, Google, StackOverflow, and the standard library are allowed.

exercises.prompt: What should you do in the first five minutes of the 45-minute coding portion?
options: Type the fastest implementation without discussing edge cases.
Read carefully, ask 3–5 clarifying questions, and restate Part 1 and its example before coding.
Start with the hardest optional part and skip the example.
Wait silently for the interviewer to provide the algorithm.
exercises.explanation: Read the prompt carefully, ask 3–5 clarifying questions (on invalid input, ordering/ties, rounding, or edge boundaries), and restate Part 1 and its example in your own words before typing code.

exercises.prompt: What should you do if you forget a Kotlin standard-library method name during the interview?
options: Stay silent until the method comes back.
Use AI-generated code despite the rules.
Say what you want to do, check the allowed stdlib reference, or write a clear 3-line loop.
Invent a method name and hope it compiles.
exercises.explanation: Say out loud what you want to do and either check your open Kotlin stdlib reference tab (which is explicitly allowed) or write a clean 3-line `for` loop so you never stall in silence.

exercises.prompt: What is the 3-minute stall rule during the coding screen?
options: After 3 minutes, rewrite the whole solution silently.
After 3 minutes, conceal the bug until the end.
After 3 minutes, state what you expected, what you see, and what you will test next, or ask for a sanity check.
exercises.explanation: If you are stuck on a bug or requirement for more than 3 minutes, state out loud what you expected, what you are seeing, and what you are testing next—or ask the interviewer to sanity-check your assumption.

exercises.prompt: In the final loop's AI Programming interview, what is the golden rule before accepting AI-generated code?
options: Ask for a plan, request small typed functions, read every line, test missed edge cases, and explain why you trust it.
Accept the first answer and avoid reviewing it.
Ask for one giant generic function and skip tests.
Use `Double` for money so generated code is shorter.
exercises.explanation: Ask for a plan first, request small scoped functions using your own types (`Long` cents, `data class`), read every single line before accepting it, test the edge cases the AI missed, and be ready to explain why you trust the code.
